summary: Defines RIFT, a specialized dynamic routing protocol for Clos and fat tree topologies and their variants. Such topologies suit constructing IP fabrics in data centers, and the protocol is optimized for them.

eli5.summary: Data center networks look like a tree with many branches. RIFT is a way for the switches to learn the roads that is designed for exactly that shape.

questions: what is routing in fat trees
how does rift differ from ospf and bgp
what is a fallen leaf in rift
subtitle: A routing protocol built for data center Clos and fat tree fabrics: link-state going up, distance-vector going down.

tldr.problem: Data center IP fabrics are built as Clos or fat tree topologies, and their builders want a routing protocol that configures itself, keeps very little state and copes with failures without human help.
tldr.mechanism: RIFT floods link-state information only northbound, so each level sees the topology below it, while each node sends a default route southbound like a distance-vector protocol. When failures would make a default route drop traffic, nodes automatically disaggregate the affected prefixes.
tldr.outcome: Leaves normally hold little more than a load-balanced default route, forwarding is valley-free and loop-free, and optional Zero Touch Provisioning can derive levels with almost no configuration. It is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025.

today: RFC 9692 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. The companion document RFC 9696 covers applicability and operational considerations.

sections.title: Why a Protocol for Fat Trees
sections.content:
Clos topologies, often called fat trees in IP fabric discussions, have become common as computation and storage move into centralized data centers. Their builders want a protocol that configures itself and deals with failures and misconfigurations with a minimum of human intervention, so that fabric bandwidth can be consumed in a "standard component" fashion.

RIFT does not tweak a link-state or a distance-vector protocol. It mixes both: "link-state towards the spines" and "distance vector towards the leaves". Bottom levels flood their link-state information north, while each node generates a default route and floods it south. This naturally supports address aggregation, but aggregation can drop traffic during failures, so RIFT adds automatic disaggregation of prefixes on link and node failures.

The RFC also lists optional fully automated topology construction, minimal routing state, automatic pruning and balancing of flooding, loop-free forwarding, fast mobility, bandwidth-based traffic rebalancing and a small key-value datastore.
sections.eli5: Big computer rooms are wired like a tree. RIFT is a way for the switches to learn the roads on their own, with a design made for exactly that shape.

sections.title: Levels, Planes and Directions
sections.content:
RIFT needs a topology with a sense of top and bottom. A level is the set of nodes at the same height. A leaf sits at level 0 in RIFT, and the Top of Fabric (ToF) is the set of nodes with no northbound adjacencies. Between them are spines. A Point of Delivery (PoD) is a self-contained vertical slice, normally holding only level 0 and level 1 nodes, and ToF nodes belong to no PoD. Moving toward the top is northbound, and toward the bottom is southbound.

In large fabrics, or fabrics made from low-radix switches, the ToF may be split into several independent planes. The RFC describes a single-plane three-level topology and a multi-plane variant. Multi-plane fabrics need extra concepts such as negative disaggregation.

Links between nodes at the same level are called East-West links. Leaf-to-leaf shortcuts (L2L) are East-West links at the leaf level.
sections.eli5: Think of floors in a building. Floor 0 is the ground floor with the leaves, and the roof is the top. Some very big buildings are split into separate towers, called planes.

sections.title: Information Flow: North TIEs and South TIEs
sections.content:
RIFT's defining property is that link-state information is flooded only northbound, so each level learns the full topology of the levels south of it. Information is not flooded East-West or back south, with exceptions such as south reflection. Southbound, normally just a default route travels one hop, and those nodes then generate their own routing information to flood further south.

The link-state database is therefore split into North TIEs and South TIEs. A TIE (Topology Information Element) describes parts of the network, such as links and prefixes, and always has a direction and a type. North TIEs hold a node's adjacencies and local prefixes. South TIEs hold its adjacencies, the default prefix, any disaggregated prefixes and local prefixes.

Because nodes do not get the same reachability from several directions, RIFT does not need to tie-break by distance. Southbound forwarding is always preferred, which gives valley-free forwarding: a packet may turn from north to south, and may cross a horizontal link at most once during its northbound phase. This guarantees loop-free forwarding.
sections.eli5: Messages about what is below only travel up. Messages from above only say 'send the rest of your stuff to me'. So nobody hears the same news twice from different sides.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and Flooding
sections.content:
RIFT messages are defined in a Thrift model and carried in a security envelope inside UDP. Neighbors are found with LIE (Link Information Element) packets, sent over a well-known IPv4 multicast address or a link-local IPv6 multicast address. LIEs and TIEs MUST be sent with an IPv4 TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit of 1 or 255, and anything else is ignored, so information does not travel beyond one Layer 3 hop. The assigned UDP ports are 914 for LIEs and 915 for TIEs.

An adjacency moves from OneWay to TwoWay to ThreeWay as the two sides see and reflect each other in LIEs. Only a ThreeWay adjacency is advertised in Node TIEs and used for computation. A minimally valid LIE requires, among other things, the same major schema version, a valid and different System ID, a matching MTU and compatible levels.

Once adjacent, nodes exchange TIEs. TIEs are ordered by direction, originator, type, TIE number and sequence number, with lifetimes used as a final tie-break. Database synchronization uses TIDE packets, which describe the TIEs a node holds, and TIRE packets, which request missing TIEs and confirm received ones. To cut flooding volume, a node can pick a subset of its parents as Flood Repeaters that carry its North TIEs further north.

RIFT has no special purge packet. To remove information, an originator issues a new empty version of the TIE with a higher sequence number and the short purge_lifetime, and every node ages it out on its own.
sections.eli5: Switches first say hello to the neighbor on each cable. Once both sides have confirmed they hear each other, they swap their maps. To remove old news, they just publish a blank page with a short life.

sections.title: Route Computation
sections.content:
A node conceptually runs two computations. The northbound SPF (N-SPF) uses northbound and East-West adjacencies and is really a one-hop calculation, because South Node TIEs are not reflooded beyond a single level. It finds the default route. The southbound SPF (S-SPF) uses only southbound adjacencies in South Node TIEs, never East-West ones, so a southbound packet never changes direction. Both check that links are bidirectional by matching a link from both ends, with the correct System IDs and levels.

A node originates a southbound default route under defined conditions, for example when it has computed a default route during N-SPF. A node that originates one SHOULD install a default discard route if it did not compute a default during N-SPF, so the top of the fabric drops traffic for unreachable addresses.

When several route types cover the same prefix, RIFT tie-breaks on a fixed preference scale, from discard and local prefixes down to south negative prefixes. A node can also set the overload flag, and leaves SHOULD set it on all their Node TIEs so spines do not forward traffic through them.
sections.eli5: Going up, a switch only needs to know 'which neighbor above can reach the rest'. Going down, it follows the exact roads it was told about. Nobody turns around halfway.

sections.title: Disaggregation After Failures
sections.content:
Aggregation by default route is cheap but risky: if a node can reach a prefix that a peer at its level cannot, the default route would lead some traffic to the wrong place. If a node detects that its default prefix covers prefixes reachable through it but not through other nodes at the same level, it MUST explicitly advertise them in a South TIE. This is positive disaggregation. It is not transitive, so receivers do not re-flood it.

A "fallen leaf" is a leaf reachable from only a subset of ToF nodes. In a single plane, positive disaggregation is generally enough. In a fabric partitioned into planes, a breakage can only be solved within its plane, while the plane is chosen at the leaf. RIFT therefore also uses negative disaggregation: a ToF node that cannot reach a fallen leaf SHOULD advertise negative South Prefix TIEs for the leaf's prefixes. They "punch out a hole" in a shorter positive route and propagate further south when a node has lost all routes to the prefix, so leaves can avoid the broken plane.

For this to work, the ToF nodes must share the same north topology. RIFT suggests connecting planes with bidirectional rings that reserve at least two ports on each ToF node. ToF East-West links are used only to flood control information and MUST NOT carry traffic.
sections.eli5: Usually a switch says 'send everything to me'. If it loses a road, it must say 'except for this address' or 'I cannot reach this one', so cars do not drive into a dead end.

sections.title: Zero Touch Provisioning and Further Mechanisms
sections.content:
Optional RIFT ZTP lets a node derive its level from offers received from neighbors, with no RIFT-specific configuration except marking ToF nodes (and leaves where explicitly wanted). A node starting with no level takes the numerically highest level offered, called HAL, and uses MAX(HAL-1,0) as its derived level. The fabric is numbered from the top down, and the top-of-fabric level constant is 24. ZTP can be mixed freely with manual configuration. System IDs are 64 bits and SHOULD be derived as EUI-64 values.

The RFC warns that autoconfiguration makes miscabling detection hard when leaves are not marked, and shows how an unmarked leaf can pull itself into an unwanted higher level.

Other mechanisms include mobility handling with timestamps and sequence counters, a Key/Value store for distributing non-topology data after convergence, interaction with BFD for faster link failure detection, and bandwidth-based balancing of northbound traffic. Leaf-only implementations are much simpler, since leaves hold only a default route, their own North TIEs and the South TIEs of connected level 1 nodes.
sections.eli5: Switches can work out which floor they are on by asking the neighbors above. You only have to tell the ones at the very top that they are the top.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
RIFT offers a range of security models, from a port-association model that shares a key per pair of ports, through a node-association model, to a fabric-association model with one shared secret for the whole fabric. They trade integrity for provisioning effort and may be mixed. Goals are authentication, message integrity, replay prevention, low processing overhead and efficient messaging. Message confidentiality is a non-goal, and the protocol uses fingerprints or signatures rather than encryption.

Every packet travels in a security envelope with an outer fingerprint, and TIEs carry an inner origin fingerprint. An implementation MUST implement sending and receiving HMAC-SHA256 fingerprints, though it MAY use the undefined key ID by default. Lifetimes are protected by a signature so an attacker cannot shorten them.

The Security Considerations section notes that a router changing its System ID repeatedly could pollute the network with stale TIEs, which is not unique to RIFT and should be benign given today's memory, and that a node SHOULD discard contents of TIEs absent from its SPF tree over a configurable period. It also discusses the choice of TTL or Hop Limit 1 versus 255, malformed packets, and the fact that using IPv4 broadcast or IPv6 all-routers multicast for LIEs on limited platforms is a last resort with a wider attack surface.
sections.eli5: Switches can sign their messages with a secret stamp so fake notes get thrown away. The notes are not hidden, just stamped.

layers.label: Level 1: Spines
layers.detail: Top of PoD; flood North TIEs further north

layers.label: Level 0: Leaves
layers.detail: Hold a load-balanced default route; attach prefixes

cells: All of the node's adjacencies and local prefixes
Southbound (and East-West, except at the ToF)
All adjacencies, the default prefix, necessary disaggregated prefixes and local prefixes

messages.label: LIE
messages.note: Discovery until both sides reflect each other (ThreeWay).

messages.label: TIRE
messages.note: Requests missing TIEs and confirms received ones.

left.title: Positive disaggregation
left.desc: Originated by a router that can still reach the prefix. Not transitive: receivers do not re-flood it.

right.title: Negative disaggregation
right.desc: Says the origin cannot reach a prefix. Can be transitive and propagate south, punching a hole in a shorter positive route.

items.title: Port-Association Model
items.text: A shared key or key pair for each pair of directly connected ports.

items.title: Node-Association Model
items.text: Controls connectivity between entire nodes and simplifies port sparing.

items.title: Fabric-Association Model
items.text: A single shared secret across the fabric controls which nodes join.

items.title: Zero configuration
items.text: Rely on ZTP and adjacencies between nodes in adjacent levels.
